column1: # refusal-range-edges.tsv — the values every binding must answer the
# same way, and that no corpus sample holds.
# `docs/OPEN-ITEMS.md` (Guards): the corpus sweep is the executable
# contract for the wire answers — 3760 cells per language, octet by
# octet — and it says nothing about the values a sample never holds.
# Both defects the last pass through `endpoints/c` found were of that
# kind (`-0.0`, a bitset holder wider than its anchor), and no second
# file of reference octets would have caught them: the corpus *cannot*
# carry these values, because `wireprobe-endpoint-gen` refuses a sample
# that does not fit its member before a renderer sees it. The gap was
# that refusals and range edges had no case list at all. This file is
# that list.
# One row per edge. Each row has exactly one right answer, derived from
# the named clause and not from any implementation, and every binding —
# the fifteen endpoint bindings, the three runtime columns, the probe —
# has to give it. `answer` is either
#   refuse       the call reports an error and writes nothing. *How* is
#                the binding's own idiom — a compile-time type error, an
#                exception, an error return — and any of those is the
#                same answer. Octets are the wrong answer: a masked,
#                truncated or canonicalised value on the wire is the
#                silent-drop class (`put_u16(70000)` -> `7011`).
#   <hex>        the exact octets, on a little-endian stream at offset 0
#                from a fresh writer. For these rows a refusal is the
#                wrong answer: the value has an exact form in the width
#                and refusing it refuses a value the type system holds.
# `tools/wireprobe/endpoint-number-surface` already asks the four
# integer rows of the fifteen endpoint bindings and exits 8 when a
# binding answers `over-u16` with octets; the remaining rows are the
# same treatment for every other operation, written down first so the
# later tests measure against the clause and not against each binding's
# own habits.
# edge
over-u8
column6: Byte/Int8/UInt8 occupy one octet; 256 has no 8-bit form. Masking to 0x00 drops the whole value without a word.

column1: over-u16
column6: 0x11170 has no 16-bit form. The masked 0x1170 ("7011") is the recorded defect class: seven bindings answered it with octets before the surface check existed.

column1: over-u32
negative-u16
column6: -12345 is exactly 0xCFC7 in sixteen bits. Octets are the right answer here: a binding that refuses every negative `short` cannot carry the IDL type at all.

column1: negative-u32
column6: -1234567 is 0xFFED2979 — the corpus's own value, `vendor_bytes.md` `mixed`, three vendors.

column1: past-2-63
column6: 0xDEADBEEFDEADC2BE is exact in 64 unsigned bits. A binding that routes it through a signed 64-bit intermediate refuses it or flips it; both are the binding's arithmetic and not the caller's value.

column1: negative-zero-f32
column6: -0.0 and +0.0 are distinct IEEE 754 values with distinct bit patterns. A binding that canonicalises writes 00000000 — different octets for the value the caller passed. Found once in `endpoints/c`.

column1: negative-zero-f64
column6: The same edge at eight octets.

column1: char-above-8-bit
column6: No measured front end can even be handed a Char8 above U+00FF — the value is unrepresentable before any serialiser runs. Narrowing writes a character nobody wrote.

column1: wchar-above-bmp
column5: XTypes 1.3 Table 31 (Char16 is one 16-bit unit), §7.4.1.1.2 (surrogate pairs are the wstring's; inventory D5)
column6: A scalar Char16 cannot carry a supplementary code point. Fast DDS's answer — truncate to sixteen bits — is the recorded wrong value D5 names.

column1: member-id-past-28-bit
column6: The header formula masks the id, so writing a larger one aliases the member onto `id & 0x0FFFFFFF` — a well-formed header for the wrong member, unreadably silent.

column1: short-pid-past-0x3f00
column4: refuse the short form; write PID_EXTENDED
column5: XTypes 1.3 §7.4.1.2.2 (short-form ids 0 to 0x3F00 inclusive; 0x3F01-0x3FFF reserved; inventory I12, I14)
column6: A short pid in the reserved range collides with the protocol's own parameters — PID_EXTENDED is 0x3F01 itself. Id 0x3F00 exactly still takes the short form; the off-by-one was a recorded defect (I12).

column1: fixed-digits-past-31
column5: OMG IDL 4.2 §7.4.1.4.4.3.4 rule (42) (digits capped at 31; inventory P4)
column6: The BCD rule is defined up to 31 digits; every measured ORB family refuses past it.

column1: fixed-scale-past-digits
column5: OMG IDL 4.2 §7.4.1.4.4.3.4 rule (42) (the scale shall not exceed the digits; inventory P4)
column6: The declaration names a value the type cannot hold.

column1: bitset-anchor-width
column5: XTypes 1.3 CommonBitfield (`holder_type` must be a primitive integer type), Table 31 (widths 8/16/32/64; inventory P1)
column6: The anchor is the smallest of 1, 2, 4 or 8 octets that holds the whole chain — here four. Three octets is a width no `holder_type` can name and no reader can be told about; a holder wider than the anchor was found once in `endpoints/c`.

column1: lc-body-size-mismatch
column6: Under LC 0..3 the code *is* the length. A body of another size misdeclares it and the reader's skip lands inside data; LC 4..7 exist for every other size, so there is never a reason to lie.

column1: frame-past-0xffff
column5: DDS-XRCE 1.0 §8.3 (submessage_length is a 16-bit count; §8.3.5.14 FRAGMENT is the path for more)
column6: A wrapped length is put_u16(70000) at frame scale: the header promises 0 octets and the peer reads the payload as the next frame. `endpoints/c` returns 0 here; a frame writer that ran past its own buffer was a recorded defect in one binding.
